NVLink SHARP on H100 · NCCL 2.32.3 · experiments of 18–19 November 2026

The hidden packets of NVLS AllReduce

NCCL can sum data inside the NVLink switch instead of passing it around a ring of GPUs. On paper this needs far fewer bytes per GPU. In practice it gains much less than the byte count promises. Nine experiments trace the missing speed to two small kinds of packet that the ring algorithm never sends.

A report on the root-cause series of the scale-up communication observability project. It assumes no earlier knowledge of the project or of GPU communication.

1.31× of 1.56×Measured speed-up of NVLS AllReduce over Ring at 8 GPUs, against what byte counts allow
w = 1.343Wire cost (wire bytes ÷ data bytes) of NVLS AllReduce at 4 GPUs, against w = 1.135 for one multimem operation alone
0.231 S + 0.125 SRead requests and write responses, as multiples of the buffer size S, that land on directions already full of data
1.45×Gain over Ring at 8 GPUs if those two packet kinds did not exist (accounting with measured wire bytes); the bound is 1.56×

Background: moving data between GPUs

Links, a switch, and two directions

The machine has eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Each GPU connects to a set of NVSwitch chips by 18 NVLink lanes. In this report we treat a GPU's lanes together as one link with two directions: sent (out of the GPU) and received (into the GPU). The two directions are separate wires, so a GPU can send and receive at full speed at the same time. Engineers call this full duplex.

On this machine, one direction of one GPU's link carries at most about 420–427 GB/s of traffic, counting everything on the wire. That number appears again and again below: it is the ceiling every pattern hits.

AllReduce, two ways

Training a model on several GPUs needs an operation called AllReduce: every GPU has a buffer of numbers, and at the end every GPU must hold the element-by-element sum of all buffers. NVIDIA's library NCCL offers two ways to do it on one machine.

  • Ring. The GPUs form a circle. Each GPU passes pieces of its buffer to its neighbour, adds what it receives, and passes the result on. After 2(N−1) steps every GPU has the full sum. Each direction of each GPU carries D = 2(N−1)/N × S of data: 1.5 S at 4 GPUs, 1.75 S at 8.
  • NVLS (NVLink SHARP). The switch itself can add and copy. Two special GPU instructions use this. multimem.ld_reduce asks the switch to read the same address on every GPU, add the values, and return the sum. multimem.st sends one store to the switch, which writes it into every GPU. NCCL's kernel gives each GPU 1/N of the buffer: the GPU sums its share with ld_reduce, then writes the result to everyone with multimem.st. Each direction of each GPU then carries D = (1 + 1/N) × S: 1.25 S at 4 GPUs, 1.125 S at 8.

If both methods could run their links at the same speed, NVLS would be faster by the ratio of bytes:

GPUsRing, data factor k = 2(N−1)/NNVLS, data factor k = 1 + 1/NBest possible speed-up (ratio of k)
41.51.251.20×
81.751.1251.56×

What actually travels on a link: packets

Data does not move as a plain stream of bytes. It moves in packets. A data packet has a header (where it goes, what it is) and up to 128 bytes of data. Some operations also need small packets without data:

  • A read needs a read request ("send me these bytes") that travels the opposite way from the data it asks for.
  • Some writes must be acknowledged. The receiver then sends back a write response. Ordinary stores on this machine get almost none; we will see that multimem.st gets one per packet.

Every packet without data, and every header, takes link time that data cannot use. Because a link direction has a fixed ceiling, the more of these bytes a pattern needs per byte of data, the less data it can move per second. This is the whole story of this report.

How we count

Every experiment measures bytes on each GPU's link, separately for the two directions. Two counters in the GPU driver do this, and they run on the same links at the same time:

InstrumentWhat it countsName used below
nvidia-smi nvlink -gt dPayload only: the bytes the instructions asked to movedata counter
nvidia-smi nvlink -gt rEverything on the wire: payload, headers, requests, responses, and link-level bytesraw counter
Nsight Systems GPU metrics (from experiment 3 on)Bytes of four packet types per direction: request data, request protocol, response data, response protocol, 10 000 samples per secondpacket counters

From these counters and the work the program records, this page uses three kinds of bytes, each with one name:

NameSymbolWhat it isCounted by
Buffer bytes (payload)The size of the collective's buffer: what the user asked to reduce or gather. Not a link quantityThe program: 4 × the mean bytes each GPU finished of its own quarter (nccl-tests: buffer size × calls)
Data bytesThe user's numbers that cross one direction of one GPU's link (the data part of data packets)Data counter
Wire bytes (raw)Everything that crosses that direction: data, packet headers, control packets (read requests, write responses), anything elseRaw counter; the packet counters split it into packet types

Writing convention. Anything counted on one direction is written as a multiple of the buffer size . "" means: for a buffer of bytes, that direction carried 1.135 × wire bytes. Packet types are written the same way, for example "0.231 of read requests".

Two ratios connect the three, and they are the only ratios this page uses:

RatioDefinitionWhat sets it
Data factor The algorithm alone: AllGather and ReduceScatter 1 on the busy direction; NVLS AllReduce ; Ring AllReduce . The data counter always matches it
Wire cost The packets: = 1.13 means 13% of the wire time carried something other than data

And three rates: algBW = ; data rate = (on the busier direction this is busBW); wire rate = . In our program, algBW is measured from the work the CTAs finish and the GPU clock, and the data rate and wire rate from the driver counters divided by the window time; they are three separate measurements. How nccl-tests runs differ is given in the last section.

The driver counters run for the whole program, including start-up and checks. So each setting runs twice, a long run (11 windows of 300 ms) and a short run (3 windows), and every count is taken as long − short: exactly 8 windows, 2.4 s of work. Values are computed per GPU and round; tables and charts show the median over 4 GPUs × 3 rounds. The profiler needs no subtraction: it timestamps its samples, and only samples inside the measured kernels are kept.

Worked example

One GPU (GPU 4), one round, multimem.st alone on all 4 GPUs. Long − short, the four GPUs processed S = 901.5 GB of buffer.

StepSent (GPU → switch)Received (switch → GPU)

W ÷ D (wire cost w)3.8521.135

The received direction carries every GPU's stores (D = 1.000 S): 375.6 GB/s of data at 426.2 GB/s wire rate. The sent direction carries only this GPU's own stores (D ≈ 0.25 S), yet its W is far larger than that.

Busy and low-data directions

When one multimem operation runs alone on every GPU, its two link directions are used very differently. One direction carries the main data stream; we call it the busy direction. The other carries only this GPU's own quarter of the data (at 4 GPUs); we call it the low-data direction. It is not idle: it also carries headers, the operation's small packets, and some wire bytes that no packet counter sees.

One operation aloneBusy direction (D = S)Low-data direction (D = S/N = 0.25 S at 4 GPUs)
multimem.stReceived: the switch writes every GPU's stores into this GPUSent: this GPU's own stores, plus write responses
ld_reduceSent: this GPU answers the switch's reads for every GPU's sumsReceived: this GPU's own sums, plus read requests

"Low-data-direction traffic" means the wire bytes W of that direction, as a multiple of S or per second.

The puzzle

Earlier measurements on this machine found two problems that this series set out to explain.

Problem 1: running both multimem operations at once is slow. On 4 GPUs, NVLS AllGather (only multimem.st) moved 374.5 GB/s per busiest link direction, and NVLS ReduceScatter (only ld_reduce) moved 357.0 GB/s. NVLS AllReduce, which does both, moved only 316.5 GB/s: 0.865 of the mean of the two. That loss happens whether the same or different thread blocks issue the two instructions. A full-duplex link gives no reason for it: AllReduce fills both directions, but each direction should still reach its own ceiling.

Problem 2: NVLS gains less over Ring than the byte count promises. At 8 GiB per GPU, NVLS AllReduce reached 250.7 GB/s against Ring's 244.0 on 4 GPUs (1.03×, best possible 1.20×), and 275.7 against 210.2 on 8 GPUs (1.31×, best possible 1.56×). In both cases NVLS keeps only about 0.84–0.86 of its theoretical advantage. A report from a colleague on newer B300 GPUs saw the gain almost disappear.

The first clue came from the raw counter on 8 GPUs. Every pattern, Ring or NVLS, AllGather or AllReduce, ran its busiest direction at the same wire rate, about 422 GB/s. NVLS AllReduce was not slower on the wire. It simply carried more bytes that are not data: a wire cost w = 1.36, against w = 1.16 for Ring AllReduce.

The question of this series: which packets does each multimem operation put on each link direction, and why does NVLS AllReduce have a wire cost w ≈ 1.35 when every other pattern has 1.13–1.18? The same number explains both problems.

The test bench

Most experiments use a small program written for this study instead of NCCL itself. It lets us choose exactly which instruction each thread block issues, and how many. The last experiment repeats the key measurement with NCCL's own kernels.

ItemSetting
GPUs4 × H100 80 GB (GPUs 4–7) for the first eight experiments; all 8 for the last
MemoryBuffers allocated and registered through NCCL 2.32.3 as a symmetric window, so multimem instructions work on them, exactly as in NCCL's own NVLS AllReduce kernel
Work unitA CTA (thread block) runs on one of the GPU's 132 streaming multiprocessors. Each CTA has a role: multimem.st, ld_reduce, both (AllReduce), plain store to the next GPU, or plain load from it
Default size32 CTAs × 512 threads per role, enough to reach the ceiling; each thread moves 16 bytes per instruction, 8 at a time, with the 32 threads of a warp touching consecutive addresses (NCCL's pattern)
TimingAll CTAs on all GPUs start together and run for a fixed 300 ms window, then stop. A fixed time, not a fixed byte count, keeps both operations of a mix running for the whole window
ChecksEvery word written is checked after each window. All 289 runs in this report had zero wrong words

Removing set-up traffic

The driver counters run for the whole program, including start-up and checks. So every setting runs twice: a long run (11 windows) and a short run (3 windows). Long minus short leaves exactly 8 windows of work. The profiler needs no such trick: it records timestamps, so we keep only samples taken while the measured kernel ran.

Cross-checks that hold in every experiment

  • The data counter always equals what the algorithm must move (for example D = 1.25 S for NVLS AllReduce at 4 GPUs), to four digits.
  • Repeated runs agree within 1% for every value, so tables show medians without error bars.
  • The profiler sometimes lost the counters of one to four of a GPU's 18 links (its data bytes came out at exactly 17/18, 16/18, …). Such GPUs are left out of the medians: 46 of 976 rows.
Experiment 1 of 9 · raw link bytes

Are the links busy or idle?

Motivation

On 8 GPUs every pattern hit the same wire-rate ceiling, so the loss was bytes that are not data, not idle time. Problem 1 was measured on 4 GPUs with the data counter only. If the 4-GPU loss had a different cause, for example the switch pausing when it must add and copy at once, the mixed patterns would show a lower wire rate.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
The pattern: multimem.st alone, ld_reduce alone, both in the same CTAs (AllReduce), both in separate CTAs, plain store, plain load, plain load + plain store4 GPUs, all issuing; 32 CTAs × 512 threads per role; 16 bytes per thread per memory instruction; long and short runs; 3 rounds

Procedure

  1. Run each pattern long and short, back to back, three times, rotating the order.
  2. For each GPU and direction, compute D and W from the long-minus-short difference.
  3. Take the busiest direction of each pattern and compare its wire rate W ÷ t and its wire cost w = W ÷ D.

Results

Interpretation

  • No link is idle. Every multimem pattern ran its busy direction at a wire rate of 425–427 GB/s, AllReduce included. The switch does not stall when it must add and copy at the same time.
  • AllReduce moves less data because a quarter of its wire time is something else: w = 1.343, against w = 1.135 for multimem.st alone and w = 1.189 for ld_reduce alone. With a fixed wire rate, data rate = wire rate ÷ w: 426.9 ÷ 1.343 ≈ 317.9 GB/s. The 4-GPU and 8-GPU problems have the same shape.
  • A surprise for later: alone, each operation puts W = 0.96 S (multimem.st) or 1.12 S (ld_reduce) on its low-data direction. If the mix simply added those to the busy direction of the other, AllReduce would need about W = 2 S per direction. It needs only W = 1.68 S. Something shrinks when the two operations share a link.
Experiment 2 of 9 · issue rate

Does protocol traffic follow requests or time?

Motivation

Alone, each operation puts about W = 1 S of wire bytes on its low-data direction (defined in the background section), although only D = 0.25 S of it is data. That traffic could be of two kinds. It could be one small packet per request, which would grow and shrink with the work. Or it could be housekeeping that the link sends at a fixed rate whatever the work, such as credits that tell the other end how much room is left. Fixed-rate traffic would make the "cost per request" look larger than it is, and could explain why the mix seems cheaper.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
How hard one operation pushes: CTAs × threads from 1 × 32 up to 32 × 512, for multimem.st alone and ld_reduce alone. The rate actually reached is measured, not assumed4 GPUs, all issuing; 16 bytes per thread per memory instruction; long and short runs; 3 rounds

Procedure

  1. Run 6 settings of multimem.st and 5 of ld_reduce, long and short, three rounds.
  2. On each GPU, read the raw counter of each direction before and after every run; long minus short gives the bytes of 8 windows (2.4 s).
  3. Divide by the buffer bytes S of those windows (W ÷ S) and by 2.4 s (wire rate). The busy direction is received for multimem.st and sent for ld_reduce; the low-data direction is the other one.
  4. Plot both directions against the data rate reached on the busy direction. The raw counter gives one total per direction, so this experiment cannot tell which kind of bytes grow; experiments 3, 4 and 6 split them.

Results

Interpretation

  • It follows requests, not time. As the multimem.st data rate rose 12-fold, the wire rate of the low-data direction rose with it, from 36 to 359 GB/s, and its W stayed between 0.96 S and 1.11 S. ld_reduce behaves the same way. Fixed-rate housekeeping is ruled out.
  • But the wire cost falls when the link is busier. On the busy direction of multimem.st, w fell from 1.71 to 1.135, and for ld_reduce from 1.62 to 1.189. We expected it to stay constant. The link packs its traffic more tightly when more is waiting.
Experiment 3 of 9 · instrument check

Can we count packets by type?

Motivation

The driver counters tell us how many bytes, not which kind. Nsight Systems can split each direction into four packet types: request data, request protocol, response data and response protocol. Before trusting it we must check that it agrees with the driver counters and does not slow the work down.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
Profiler on or off, for multimem.st alone, ld_reduce alone and plain store4 GPUs; 32 CTAs × 512 threads; 11 windows; 3 rounds; custom metric set with byte sums at 10 000 samples per second

Procedure

  1. Run each pattern with and without the profiler, back to back.
  2. Compare the rates; compare the profiler's sums inside the measured kernels with the driver's counters.

Results

PatternRate with / without profiler, GB/sPackets ÷ raw counter, busy directionPackets ÷ raw counter, low-data direction
multimem.st alone93.6 / 93.699.9%43%
ld_reduce alone89.2 / 89.399.8%41%
Plain store371.5 / 371.4both directions busy, 99.4–99.5%

Interpretation

  • The profiler is safe to use. Rates change by at most 0.02%, and its data bytes equal the driver's data counter.
  • On a busy direction the four packet types are the whole raw counter. On a low-data direction they are only about 40% of it. The rest is counted by the driver but by no packet counter. We call it wire bytes outside the packets, and it matters below. The profiler cannot say what it is. A likely candidate is link-level traffic, such as acknowledgements or partly filled transfer units, sent when there is no data to share them with.
  • One planned extra, a counter of busy link cycles, was accepted by the tool but silently not recorded.
Experiment 4 of 9 · packet anatomy

The packets of each operation alone

Motivation

To understand the mix, we first need each operation's own packets on both directions. One guess from the 8-GPU numbers was that each thread's 16-byte memory instruction leaves the GPU as its own packet, with no merging. That would make the headers very expensive.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
The operation: multimem.st, ld_reduce, plain store, plain load, each issued by every GPU4 GPUs; 32 CTAs × 512 threads; each thread moves 16 bytes per memory instruction, warp-contiguous addresses; profiler on; 3 rounds

Procedure

  1. Run each operation with the profiler.
  2. For each direction, divide the bytes of each packet type by the buffer bytes S; add the wire bytes of the raw counter that fall outside every packet type.

Results

Interpretation

  • The instructions of a warp are merged into 128-byte packets. Request protocol is 0.125 S when 1.000 S of data is written: 16 header bytes per 128 data bytes. The guess of one packet per 16-byte access was wrong.
  • Every multimem.st packet is acknowledged. Its sent direction carries 0.125 S of write responses, one 16-byte response per 128-byte packet. Plain stores, the kind Ring uses, get almost none: 0.003 S.
  • ld_reduce needs read requests. To serve the other GPUs' sums, the switch sends each GPU 0.154 S of read requests, on the low-data direction.
  • Most of the low-data direction is wire bytes outside the packets: 0.550 S and 0.662 S.
Experiment 5 of 9 · instruction width and address pattern

Does the way threads address memory matter?

Motivation

If packets follow the instructions, narrower accesses would mean more packets and more headers per byte. If packets follow memory lines, width would not matter but the arrangement of addresses would. This tells us whether a different kernel could avoid the extra packets.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
Bytes per access: 4, 8, 16; address pattern: warp-contiguous (the 32 threads of a warp touch consecutive addresses, as NCCL does) or thread-contiguous (each thread works on its own run of 8 consecutive pieces, so the 32 threads of one instruction touch addresses far apart)4 GPUs; 32 CTAs × 512 threads; 8 accesses in flight per thread in every setting; profiler on; 3 rounds

Procedure

  1. Run 3 widths × 2 patterns for multimem.st and ld_reduce, and both patterns for plain load and store.
  2. Sum all non-data bytes over both directions (protocol plus wire bytes outside the packets), ÷ S.

Results

Interpretation

  • Width does not matter in NCCL's pattern. 4-, 8- and 16-byte instructions give the same packets and the same rate (374.4 GB/s for multimem.st). The GPU merges the instructions of a warp's 32 threads into 128-byte packets whatever their width.
  • Scattering the threads' addresses is much worse. Each thread's instruction becomes its own packet, and at 4 and 8 bytes each small access also fills at least a 16-byte data slot, so those points include padding: non-data bytes rise from 0.84 S to 3.42 S for multimem.st, and its rate falls 2.3-fold to 164.6 GB/s. Plain stores fall 2.8-fold.
  • NCCL's kernel already uses the cheapest pattern. No change of instruction width or address order inside the kernel can remove the write responses or the read requests.
Experiment 6 of 9 · the core test

The packets of the mix

Motivation

This is the experiment the others prepare for. Experiment 1 showed that the mix carries much less than the two operations put on their low-data directions alone. Three explanations were on the table: packets combine when a direction is busy; part of the empty-direction traffic is not per request (ruled out by experiment 2); or packets get smaller. Counting each packet type inside the mix itself decides it.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
Mixed or alone: AllReduce (both operations in the same 32 CTAs), both in separate CTAs (32 + 32), and each operation alone as reference4 GPUs; 512 threads per CTA; 16-byte instructions, warp-contiguous addresses; profiler on; 5 rounds, order rotated

Procedure

  1. Run the four arms interleaved, five rounds.
  2. For each direction, add the packets of the two operations alone and compare with the packets of the mix.
  3. Do the same for the wire bytes outside the packets.

Results

Direction (all values × S)Packets, alone: st + ld_reducePackets, AllReduceDifferenceOutside packets, alone → mixed
Sent0.406 + 1.187 = 1.5931.594+0.0000.55 → 0.076
Received1.134 + 0.456 = 1.5901.667+0.0770.66 → 0.012

Interpretation

  • The packets add up. On the sent direction, AllReduce's packets equal the sum of the two operations alone to three decimals. On the received direction they are slightly more (+0.077 S), all in read requests: 0.231 S in the mix against 0.154 S alone.
  • What vanishes is the traffic outside the packets. It is large only on a low-data direction and shrinks to almost nothing when data fills the direction. So the "missing" bytes of experiment 1 were never part of the cost of the mix.
  • This is the cause. Each busy direction of AllReduce carries, on top of its data and data headers, the small packets the other operation used to hide on its low-data direction: the switch's read requests on the received side (0.231 S) and the responses to multicast writes on the sent side (0.125 S). Together with headers and the few wire bytes outside the packets, this gives a wire cost w = 1.343 (received) and w = 1.336 (sent). Ring needs neither kind: plain stores are not acknowledged and Ring never reads remotely.
  • Same or separate CTAs make no difference, because the packets are formed below the CTAs, in the GPU's link interface and the switch.
Experiment 7 of 9 · sharing

Who gets the link when both want it?

Motivation

An earlier test suggested that read replies keep their speed while multicast stores take what is left, as if reads had priority. If there were a priority rule, a kernel might be tuned around it.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
How many CTAs issue each operation: ld_reduce at 0, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 CTAs with multimem.st at 32; and the reverse4 GPUs, all issuing both; 512 threads per CTA; separate CTAs per operation; 3 rounds

Procedure

  1. Run the 11 settings, three rounds each.
  2. Plot each operation's rate (bytes of its own share per GPU per second) against the other operation's CTA count.

How the rate of each operation is measured

The rate comes from the work the CTAs finish and the GPU clock, not from the link counters.

  • What counts. Each GPU works on its own quarter of the buffer. Each CTA walks its slice of that quarter in chunks of 1 MiB and counts the chunks it finished. One byte of the GPU's own quarter counts once, even though multimem.st writes it into 4 GPUs and ld_reduce sums it from 4.
  • The time. All CTAs start from one signal. After 300 ms a controller CTA raises a stop flag, and each CTA stops within two chunks. Before reading the end time, each CTA waits until its stores are delivered (__threadfence_system()).
  • The formula. Rate of one GPU = finished chunks of all CTAs of that operation × 1 MiB ÷ (latest CTA end − earliest CTA start). Then the mean over the 4 GPUs, the median over 5 windows and the median over 3 rounds.
  • Worked example. 32 + 32 CTAs, round 1, first measured window, GPU 4: the multimem.st CTAs finished 17 366 chunks in 301 330 976 ns, so 17 366 × 1 048 576 ÷ 301 330 976 = 60.43 GB/s. The mean over the 4 GPUs is 60.70; the medians over windows and rounds give 60.7 GB/s.
  • Link to the link counters. With one operation alone, 4 × this rate is the data rate on its busy direction: multimem.st alone at 93.6 GB/s is 374 GB/s of data received per GPU.

Results

Interpretation

  • Nobody has priority; the share follows demand. With 64 CTAs of multimem.st against 32 of ld_reduce, stores get 73.4 GB/s and reads 41.5. Reversed, stores get 36.0 and reads 76.7. At 32 + 32 they get 60.7 and 67.5.
  • Shifting CTAs moves the split between the two operations but cannot remove the extra packets, so it is no fix.
Experiment 8 of 9 · latency

How long does one operation wait?

Motivation

The colleague's report proposed a shared limit on how many multimem requests a GPU can have in flight. Timing single operations while other traffic runs shows where requests wait, and is a first step towards testing that idea.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
Background traffic on all 4 GPUs: none, plain store, multimem.st, ld_reduce, AllReduce (32 CTAs × 512 threads each)A probe: one thread on an otherwise unused processor of each GPU issues one 16-byte operation at a time and times it; probe kinds: ld_reduce, or multimem.st followed by a fence that waits for its acknowledgement; 3 rounds; no profiler

Procedure

  1. For each background and probe kind, record the latency of every probe operation for 5 windows.
  2. Take the median and 90th percentile per GPU and window, then the median over GPUs and rounds.

Results

Interpretation

  • Requests wait much longer behind multimem traffic than behind plain stores, even though both fill the link. The delay added over idle links is 4.5 to 14 times larger under a multimem background.
  • This shows long queues, not a fixed limit. Whether a hard limit on requests in flight also exists cannot be decided from these numbers.
Experiment 9 of 9 · NCCL on 8 GPUs

Does NCCL on 8 GPUs behave the same?

Motivation

Experiments 1–8 used our own program on 4 GPUs. The final check runs NCCL's real kernels on all 8 GPUs, compares them with Ring, and connects the packets to problem 2.

Configuration

What changesWhat stays fixed
The NCCL kernel: NVLS AllGather, NVLS ReduceScatter, NVLS AllReduce (symmetric multicast kernels, 2 CTAs × 512 threads as NCCL chooses), Ring AllReduce (24 CTAs × 512 threads)All 8 GPUs; nccl-tests with 2 GiB buffers, 200 timed calls; profiler on; 3 rounds

Procedure

  1. Run each kernel under the profiler; check that the profiler does not change its speed (it changed by at most 0.2%).
  2. Keep only samples inside NCCL's kernels; divide by the calls × 2 GiB.
  3. Compare busy-direction packet bytes of NVLS and Ring AllReduce.

Results

Interpretation

  • NCCL's kernels show the same packets as our program: 16-byte headers on 128-byte data packets, one response per multicast write packet, and read requests for ld_reduce. The mix adds up in the same way.
  • Counting packets only, Ring's wire cost is w = 1.14; NVLS AllReduce's is w = 1.35 on the side where read requests arrive and w = 1.26 on the side where write responses leave. Ring's responses are only 0.028 S.
  • These two packet kinds explain about half of problem 2. All busy directions run at the same wire-rate limit C, and algBW = C ÷ (k × w) = C ÷ (W ÷ S), so the speed-up follows W ÷ S on the busier direction (driver raw counter, 8 GPUs): Ring W = 2.028 S, NVLS W = 1.530 S, ratio 1.33 (measured 1.33). Without the read requests (0.239 S) and write responses (0.125 S), NVLS would need W = 1.291 S received and 1.394 S sent: a ratio of 1.45, against the byte-count bound of 1.56. The rest of the gap is the sent side's wire bytes in no packet type (about 0.1 S), the GPU's own read requests and the headers. An earlier version of this page said 1.54 and "nearly all"; it used the packet counters only (corrected 21 November 2026).

Putting it together: what NVLS AllReduce should reach

This section first fixes the words, then derives from theory alone what NVLS AllReduce should reach, and only then compares with the measurements.

Recap: three kinds of bytes

The same three byte counts as in "How we count", with where they live:

NameSymbolWhat it isWhere it livesMeasured by
Buffer bytes (payload)The size of the collective's buffer: what the user asked to reduce or gather. Not a link quantityIn GPU memoryKnown from the call (nccl-tests: buffer size; our program: 4 × the bytes each GPU finished of its own quarter)
Data bytesThe user's numbers that cross one direction of one GPU's link: the data part of data packetsOn one link directionDriver data counter (nvidia-smi nvlink -gt d)
Wire bytes (raw)Everything that crosses that direction: data + packet headers + control packets (read requests, write acknowledgements) + anything elseOn one link directionDriver raw counter (nvidia-smi nvlink -gt ); the profiler splits it into packet types

Only two ratios are needed to connect them, and the rest of this section uses only these two:

Theory: what each collective should reach

No measured values in this subsection: only the packet rules.

  • Data packets carry d bytes of data plus a header; the header adds bytes per data byte.
  • Read requests: a read over NVLink needs a request travelling the other way. ld_reduce has two kinds, with separate symbols because they need not be the same size:
    • : the request a GPU sends to the switch for a sum of its own share (as issuer); bytes per data byte of that sum.
    • : the request the switch sends to each GPU to read its copy (the GPU as target); bytes per data byte read.
  • Write acknowledgements: a write that is acknowledged returns bytes per data byte written. Plain stores, which Ring uses: .

, , and are unknowns: no NVLink specification we have gives them, so the theory keeps them as symbols. Only the measurements below give them values.

What actually happens on the links, packet by packet

Each GPU plays two roles at once. As an issuer it runs the instruction on its own share of the buffer (/N bytes). As a target it is written to, or read from, by the switch on behalf of every GPU's instruction, so for all bytes. Follow one 128-byte piece:

Adding up over every GPU and every piece gives each GPU's traffic, which is where the three control terms come from:

OperationRole of one GPUWhat it sends (sent direction)What it receives (received direction)
multimem.stIssuer, for its /Nits writes: a few responses from the switch: 0.009 measured, fewer than one per write it issued (one per write would be = 0.031 at 4 GPUs). Small enough to leave out of the theory
Target, for all an acknowledgement for every write it receives: the writes of all GPUs:
ld_reduceIssuer, for its /Nits read-reduce requests: the sums:
Target, for all replies with its copy of every GPU's share: the switch's read requests for all GPUs' sums:
  • , acknowledgements: a GPU acknowledges the multicast writes it receives, and it receives every GPU's writes, so worth of them. The acknowledgement goes back out, on its sent direction, the direction opposite to those writes. Plain stores (Ring) are not acknowledged packet by packet (0.003 ).
  • Who acknowledges whom. The acknowledgements go from each target to the switch, not to the issuer: for each write g issues, the switch receives acknowledgements (one from each target, g included), yet g's received direction carries only 0.009 of responses, about one per 3.5 writes it issued. So the switch does not forward each acknowledgement; it appears to collect them and return fewer, combined responses to the issuer. The counters only see bytes per link direction and packet type, not who a packet is addressed to, so this attribution is an inference from the directions and the amounts. It holds for every instruction width tested (experiment 5): the sent direction always carries exactly one 16-byte acknowledgement per received write packet.
  • , the GPU's own requests: as issuer, a GPU asks the switch only for the sums of its own share, so /N worth of requests, on its sent direction.
  • , the switch's requests: to compute each sum, the switch must read that piece on every GPU. So every GPU receives read requests for all shares, worth, on its received direction, opposite to the replies it sends.
  • Why the big terms are the target terms. The switch fans each instruction out to GPUs, so a GPU does times more work as a target () than as an issuer (/N). The two control terms proportional to , and , are the ones that land on a direction that AllReduce fills with the other operation's data.
  • What is measured and what is not. The packet kinds and directions are measured. Why the switch needs acknowledgements for multicast writes is not known; one likely reason is that the switch must know when a write has reached every GPU before it can report the store as complete. Measured values: = 0.125 (one 16-byte acknowledgement per 128-byte write), the switch's requests = 0.154 (ReduceScatter run by itself), and the GPU's own requests = 0.062 ÷ 0.25 of sums = 0.25, about 32 bytes per 128-byte piece. All values, with sources, are in the table under "Theory against measurement".

What the theory says:

  1. Headers are not the cause. appears in every row; it cancels in every comparison.
  2. More data per direction is not the cause. NVLS AllReduce has , but counts data bytes, so does not enter busBW.
  3. The whole difference is the control-packet term . With (no read requests, no acknowledged writes), NVLS AllReduce would reach exactly the busBW of AllGather alone and of Ring.
  4. Alone, the control packets cost nothing. AllGather puts its acknowledgements, and ReduceScatter the switch's read requests, on the direction that carries only /N of data, where there is room. In AllReduce both directions carry of data, so there is no room left.
  5. Ring has no control term ( ≈ 0): it only writes with plain stores, and its reduction reads the GPU's own memory, not NVLink.

A reference case, not a prediction. To get a feel for the size, suppose every control packet is as large as one data-packet header and there is one per data packet. Experiment 4 measured headers of 16 bytes per 128-byte data packet ( = 0.125), so this case is , with no small responses (). Then the control term is at every , = 1.25 against 1.125, and NVLS AllReduce would reach 1.125 ÷ 1.25 = 0.90 of the busBW of AllGather alone (a 10% loss at any GPU count), and of Ring's algBW: 1.08 at 4 GPUs and 1.40 at 8. The 16 and 128 come from our own measurement, so this case only illustrates the formula; the measured ρ and are compared with it below.

What the columns mean.

  • "Run by itself": the instruction is the only one running. multimem.st by itself is NVLS AllGather; ld_reduce by itself is NVLS ReduceScatter. All GPUs issue it, nothing else is on the links (experiment 4 at 4 GPUs, experiment 9 at 8). Each parameter is then read directly from one counter: for example = the sent response protocol of AllGather (0.125 ) ÷ the writes the GPU received ().
  • "Inside AllReduce": both instructions run at the same time, as in NVLS AllReduce (experiment 6 at 4 GPUs, experiment 9 at 8). Now each counter holds packets of both instructions mixed together, and the profiler cannot tell them apart. So each parameter is found by subtraction: the counter minus the part that belongs to the other instruction, taken from the "run by itself" measurement. For example = received request protocol of AllReduce (0.356 ) − headers of the incoming writes (0.125 , from AllGather by itself) = 0.231 , ÷ the data read from this GPU ().

Why the values differ. and come out the same in both columns: those packets do not change when the other instruction runs. Only differs, because the received request-protocol counter of AllReduce is 0.077 larger than the sum of the two instructions by themselves. The subtraction assigns all of that excess to read requests. That is an assumption: the counter would look the same if, instead, some incoming writes arrived in smaller packets in the mix (more headers per byte of data). Which of the two happens, and why, is not known; it is the one part of AllReduce's packets that the instructions by themselves do not predict.

  • equals the reference case exactly: one 16-byte acknowledgement per 128-byte write packet, alone and in the mix, at both GPU counts.
  • is above the reference case when run by itself (0.154–0.160 instead of 0.125, about 1.2 requests per 128 bytes read) and grows by half in the mix (0.231–0.239). This growth is the main thing the instructions run by themselves do not predict.
  • is twice the reference case (0.25 instead of 0.125: about 32 bytes of request per 128-byte sum), but it is multiplied by /N, so it adds only 0.062 (4 GPUs) or 0.031 (8 GPUs).

Check of the theory's main assumption: do the packets of the two instructions add up?

Why this check. The theory and its third level ("parameters measured on each instruction run by itself") assume that running both instructions at once, as AllReduce does, changes nothing about the packets of either: AllReduce's packets on a direction should be exactly the packets of multimem.st by itself plus those of ld_reduce by itself on that direction.

How Ring AllReduce runs, and why it does not pay this cost

Ring also fills both link directions with data. To see why it does not lose, follow one Ring AllReduce on 4 GPUs. The buffer is cut into 4 chunks A, B, C, D, and every GPU holds its own copy of each.

So in Ring, as in NVLS AllReduce, both directions of every GPU are full of data for the whole call. The difference is in what else travels on them:

Ring AllReduceNVLS AllReduce
How data crosses the linkThe sender writes (plain stores) into the next GPU's bufferld_reduce: the switch reads from every GPU. multimem.st: the switch writes into every GPU
Where the reduction readsThe GPU's own memory, not NVLinkEvery GPU's memory, over NVLink
Control packets against the dataAlmost none: 0.024–0.028 S of write responsesA read request for every read; a 16-byte response for every 128-byte multicast write packet
Wire cost w1.16 on both directions1.34 on both directions

Ring AllReduce in the same model

Ring needs only plain stores to the next GPU, so its model has two packet parameters besides , both the plain-store counterparts of the multicast ones: , the responses a GPU sends for the stores it receives (per data byte received, like ), and , the responses a GPU receives for the stores it sends (per data byte sent, like ). With , each direction carries of data:

Ring AllReduce, directionrequest datarequest protocolresponse dataresponse protocol
sent: stores to the next GPU, responses for the stores received from the previous GPU
recv: stores from the previous GPU, responses for the stores sent to the next GPU

So on the sent direction and on the received direction, plus the wire bytes in no packet type, . No read requests and no multicast acknowledgements appear in any field.

Would running the two phases one after the other help NVLS? No. NVLS AllReduce already runs both operations at once, like Ring. If it ran ReduceScatter and then AllGather, each phase would leave one direction mostly empty: 1 ÷ (1/358 + 1/376) ≈ 183 GB/s of data per direction, far below the 318 it reaches. Separate calls were measured 1.38–1.53× slower.

AllReduce runs both storyboards at the same time on the same GPUs. Diagnosis

Root cause. NVLS AllReduce puts the small control packets of its two instructions on link directions that are already full of data: the switch's read requests for ld_reduce on each GPU's received direction, and the GPU's write responses for multimem.st on its sent direction. A direction carries a fixed number of wire bytes per second (the wire rate limit C), so every wire byte these packets use is a byte of data that does not move.

How it happens, step by step:

  1. ld_reduce is a pull. To compute a sum, the switch sends a read request into every GPU. The request arrives on the GPU's received direction; the value goes back on its sent direction.
  2. multimem.st writes are acknowledged. For every 128-byte multicast write packet a GPU receives, it sends a 16-byte response on its sent direction. Plain stores, which Ring uses, get almost none.
  3. Alone, these packets are free. In ReduceScatter alone the received direction carries only 1/N of the data, so the read requests use spare wire time. In AllGather alone the same holds for the write responses on the sent direction. The busy direction of each carries only data and headers.
  4. In AllReduce both directions are full of data. The read requests now share the received direction with the multicast writes; the write responses share the sent direction with the read replies. The wire still runs at its limit (426.9 GB/s), but less of it is data.
  5. The mix adds a little more. In AllReduce the switch sends 50% more read-request bytes than in ReduceScatter alone (0.231 S instead of 0.154 S). Why is not known.

Wire cost w, split into its parts (wire bytes of each kind ÷ D on that direction), 4 GPUs, 32 CTAs × 512 threads per operation (packet counters and raw counter, experiments 4 and 6):

The read-request and write-response rows are split from the write headers by subtraction, assuming the headers are the same as when each operation runs alone; they are estimates. As multiples of S they are 0.154 S + 0.077 S (received) and 0.125 S (sent); dividing by D = 1.25 S gives the values in the table.

  • Received side: the cost rises from 1.135 to 1.343. Read requests make 0.185 of the 0.208 rise (89%).
  • Sent side: it rises to 1.336, mostly from write responses. The two sides are almost equal, so removing only one packet kind gains nothing: the other side then limits.
  • Ring fills both directions too but sends neither packet kind: w = 1.16. That is the 15% of NVLS's byte-count advantage that is lost (1.33× instead of 1.56× at 8 GPUs).

What the measurements rule out:

Not the causeEvidence
Idle link time, a switch that stallsPhysical link rate 426.9 GB/s, the same as every other pattern (experiment 1)
More data per directionbusBW counts data bytes, so the data factor k = 1 + 1/N does not enter it; with AllGather's wire cost w AllReduce would also reach 375 GB/s
Too few CTAs, or how threads issueThe cost is the same from 4 to 64 CTAs; instruction width and NCCL's address pattern do not change the packets (experiment 5)
One operation having priorityThe share follows how many CTAs issue each operation (experiment 7)
Our test programNCCL's own kernels on 8 GPUs show the same packets (experiment 9)

Still unknown: why the read requests grow 50% in the mix (0.062 of the received-side rise); what the wire bytes in no packet type on the sent side are (0.061); and whether a different memory-ordering form of multimem.st avoids the write responses.

What this means. NVLS AllReduce being below AllGather and ReduceScatter (problem 1) is mostly what their packets predict: the single operations are not a reference AllReduce can reach, because their small packets travel free on a direction with spare room. The loss that matters for performance is against Ring (problem 2).

Takeaways

  1. The links are never idle. In every pattern, on 4 and 8 GPUs, the busy directions run at the same wire rate of about 420–427 GB/s. NVLS AllReduce is not slow on the wire; a smaller share of the wire carries data.
  2. Small packets that each operation needs end up on full directions. ld_reduce needs read requests; every multimem.st packet gets a write response. Alone, each operation sends these on the direction its data does not fill. In AllReduce both directions are full of data, so they take data's place: wire cost w = 1.343 instead of 1.135 for multimem.st alone.
  3. Compared with the operations alone, AllReduce adds almost no new packets. Only the read requests grow, by 50%. What changes is where the packets travel, not how many there are.
  4. Ring does not pay this cost. Its plain stores get almost no responses and it never reads from another GPU. This is why NVLS keeps only about 85% of its byte-count advantage: 1.31× instead of 1.56× at 8 GPUs, 1.03× instead of 1.20× at 4.
  5. Fewer CTAs do not help. The wire cost w belongs to the packets, not to the load. With fewer CTAs the GPUs ask for less and less data moves; at low load w is even higher.
  6. The kernel is not the lever. NCCL's address pattern already gives the fewest packets, the bytes per thread per instruction make no difference, and moving CTAs between the operations only changes who gets the link.
  7. Both directions must improve together. The two directions of AllReduce carry different extra traffic: read requests on the received side; write responses, the GPU's own read requests and unexplained wire bytes on the sent side. Removing the write responses alone gains nothing, because the received side then limits. Removing both packet kinds would give about +9–10% algBW, or 1.45× over Ring at 8 GPUs; the full bound needs the unexplained wire bytes gone too.
  8. What to try next. Other memory-ordering forms of multimem.st (to see whether write responses depend on them) and other ways of forming ld_reduce reads, tested together. Splitting the buffer between NVLS and Ring, or pushing data instead of reading it, cannot help by byte count. The remaining levers, unacknowledged multicast writes and larger read requests, belong to the hardware.
  9. Open questions. What the wire bytes in no packet type are; why read requests grow when mixed; and how B300 (NVLink 5) behaves.

Data: 276 runs on GPUs 4–7 (18–19 November 2026) and 13 runs on GPUs 0–7 (19 November 2026), NCCL 2.32.3.
